name: Writing Systems (Script Technologies)
region: Global (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica, Indus Valley, Crete)
summary: Symbolic notation systems — cuneiform, hieroglyphs, Chinese characters, alphabets — that abstract knowledge from place and person, enabling storage, transmission, and accumulation of information beyond human memory.

claims.statement: Writing emerged independently at least four times (Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica), each time enabling knowledge accumulation beyond the limits of oral memory and spatial encoding
Alphabetic scripts dramatically lowered the symbol count required for literacy (from thousands to under 30), democratizing access to written knowledge across social classes
Writing enabled legal codes, contracts, and administrative records that could be verified, copied, and transmitted — creating the infrastructure for governance at scale

evidence.source: Schmandt-Besserat (1996) How Writing Came About, University of Texas Press
Houston (2004) The First Writing: Script Invention as History and Process, Cambridge University Press
Goldwasser (2006) Canaanites Reading Hieroglyphs, Egypt and the Levant 16
Sass (2005) The Alphabet at the Turn of the Millennium, Tel Aviv University
Roth (1997) Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor, Scholars Press (Code of Hammurabi translation)

notes: The great abstraction layer. Living knowledge systems store data in organisms; monumental encoding stores it in stone; writing stores it in symbols that can be copied onto anything. This is the moment knowledge becomes fully portable. Note the ethical_alignment is moderate (0.5): writing also enabled centralized control, taxation, debt records, and class stratification — it is a dual-use technology. The codex already documents what came before writing (songlines, quipu, tactile coding); this entry fills the conspicuous gap of writing itself.
